questions.question: Software layer that connects applications, databases, or services to each other.
questions.explanation: Middleware brokers communication between systems that weren't designed to talk directly.

questions.question: Isolated environment where code can run without affecting the real system.
questions.explanation: Sandboxes safely test untrusted code or analyze malware.

questions.question: Standard template code repeated across many files with little change.
questions.explanation: Boilerplate is reusable scaffolding like license headers and setup blocks.

questions.question: Bug where a previously working feature breaks after an update.
questions.explanation: Regression testing exists to catch features that break after changes.

questions.question: Restructuring code internally without changing its external behavior.
questions.explanation: Refactoring improves structure and readability while keeping behavior identical.

questions.question: Urgent patch pushed to production to fix a critical bug.
questions.explanation: Hotfixes bypass the normal release cycle for severe production issues.

questions.question: Background process that runs without user interaction, often named with a trailing 'd'.
questions.explanation: Daemons like sshd provide services continuously in the background.

questions.question: Marking an API or feature as obsolete and scheduled for removal.
questions.explanation: Deprecated features still work but warn users to migrate away.

questions.question: Process of preparing and assigning IT resources like servers, VMs, or user accounts.
questions.explanation: Provisioning automates creating and configuring the resources a service needs.

questions.question: Amount of data a system successfully processes or transfers per unit of time.
questions.explanation: Throughput measures real work delivered — requests per second or bits per second.

questions.question: Repeatedly checking a server at intervals for new data or status.
questions.explanation: Polling asks 'anything new?' on a timer; webhooks push events instead.

questions.question: HTTP callback that pushes event notifications to your app automatically.
questions.explanation: Webhooks POST event data to your endpoint, removing the need to poll.

questions.question: Older code still in production that is hard to maintain or replace.
questions.explanation: Legacy code lacks tests or documentation but can't easily be removed.

questions.question: Dependence on one provider that makes switching platforms costly or difficult.
questions.explanation: Proprietary formats and deep integrations create vendor lock-in.

questions.question: Component or resource that limits a system's overall performance.
questions.explanation: Removing a bottleneck — like a slow disk — lifts the whole system's speed.
